title: Transformers Learn Latent Mixture Models In-Context via Mirror Descent
claim: Predicting the next token requires inferring which past tokens matter, by combining fixed token-pair statistics with context-dependent importance weights.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right; sentence with weighted arcs beside a color-matched matrix
description: A single wide panel. On the left, an example sentence reads 'dog that saw the bird threw the ball, and then ran to fetch'. 'dog', 'bird' and 'ball' are highlighted in blue, red and yellow. The target word 'fetch' is underlined in red. Curved arrows run from each highlighted word to the target and are labelled by weight. The blue arrow from 'dog' and the yellow arrow from 'ball' are solid and labelled 'High λ'. The red dashed arrow from 'bird' is labelled 'Low λ'. On the right, 'π* =' introduces a matrix with one color-boxed row per highlighted word. Columns are verbs: fetch, chase, roll, …, fly. The 'dog' row has 0.6 under 'fetch' and 0.3 under 'chase'. The 'ball' row has 0.5 under 'fetch' and 0.4 under 'roll'. The 'bird' row has 0.8 under 'fly'. The color coding links words, arrows and matrix rows. The eye goes first to the sentence and arrows.
caption: To predict the final word, the model must infer the causal relevance of past tokens. Our MTD framework models this by separating a static, context-free unigram (π⋆) from dynamic, context-dependent weights (λ) that are inferred in-context. The model learns to assign high weights to the causally relevant positions (’dog’) and (’ball’), activating their respective slices of the unigram (e.g., π⋆(dog, ·) favouring verbs like fetch or chase). Conversely, a low weight is assigned to the distractor (’bird’), suppressing its influence.
abstract: Sequence modelling requires determining which past tokens are causally relevant from the context and their importance: a process inherent to the attention layers in transformers, yet whose underlying learned mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we formalize the task of estimating token importance as an in-context learning problem by introducing a framework based on Mixture of Transition Distributions, where a latent variable determines the influence of past tokens on the next. The distribution over this latent variable is parameterized by unobserved mixture weights that transformers must learn in-context. We demonstrate that transformers can implement Mirror Descent to learn these weights from the context. Specifically, we give an explicit construction of a three-layer transformer that exactly implements one step of Mirror Descent and prove that the resulting estimator is a first-order approximation of the Bayes-optimal predictor. Corroborating our construction and its learnability via gradient descent, we empirically show that transformers trained from scratch learn solutions consistent with our theory: their predictive distributions, attention patterns, and learned transition matrix closely match the construction, while deeper models achieve performance comparable to multi-step Mirror Descent.
